Oh, yeah, absolutely. It's been this way for as long as I can remember. Well, I mean, it's never really gone away, but it hasn't always been this bad. Like, it's been seriously disrupting my job for about two years and two months now. That's when the construction schedule changed and the hours just got completely chaotic. We started doing these split shifts to keep up with the supply chain delays. Supply chain stuff is a nightmare right now, by the way. You order a batch of electrical panels and they tell you it's a forty-week lead time. Forty weeks! How are you supposed to build a schedule around that? Some of the ink had completely faded off because of the heat. You know how those thermal printers work? They don't even use ink, it's just heat-sensitive paper. My uncle used to work for a company that manufactured those rolls. He'd bring home boxes of the defective ones for us to draw on when we were kids. We used to hold them up to the lightbulb in my bedroom lamp to watch the paper turn black. My mom got so mad because I accidentally left one on the lampshade and it started smoking. That lamp was this ugly brass thing she got at a garage sale. She loved going to garage sales. Every Saturday morning, she'd be up at 6 AM circling ads in the newspaper...\n\nBut, uh, yeah. Starting things is a huge problem. I just... I can't seem to get the engine turning over, you know?\n\nDoctor: Are your symptoms causing significant problems in your relationships with friends and family?\n\nPatient: Yeah, they definitely are. Like I was saying, it's... it's causing a lot of friction. My wife, she's just exhausted from it. I tell her I'm going to take care of something, and I really mean to, but then I just don't. And she has to remind me over and over. She shouldn't have to be my manager, you know? \n\nSpeaking of managers, the guy I report to at work, Dave... he actually sat me down a couple weeks ago. The missed follow-ups and the way I've been organizing—or not organizing—the site coordination, it's gotten bad enough that he had to express formal concern. Dave's usually a pretty laid-back guy, too. He used to manage this huge commercial development downtown before he came to our company. That project was massive, like three city blocks. They had to pour so much concrete for the foundation, they had trucks lined up around the block starting at 3 AM. You have to pour early in the summer so the concrete doesn't cure too fast in the heat. If it cures too fast, it cracks, and then you've got a whole structural nightmare on your hands. My buddy Steve poured a patio in his backyard last July right in the middle of the day, and I told him, I said, \"Steve, you gotta wait till the evening or keep it wet.\" He didn't listen, and sure enough, two weeks later, giant hairline crack right down the middle. He tried to patch it with some epoxy filler, but you can always see the patch. It never matches the original color. Concrete's funny like that, the color depends on the exact mix of sand and aggregate...\n\nBut, uh, anyway. Yeah, my wife is worn out, and my boss is seriously worried about my work. It's a mess.\n\nDoctor: Are you having trouble completing everyday tasks, like household chores or personal care, because of your symptoms?\n\nPatient: Yeah, chores, work tasks... it all kind of falls apart halfway through. Like, take work for example. If someone gives me a list of things to follow up on after a site walk... Site walks are usually first thing in the morning, right when the dew is still heavy. You definitely need good waterproof boots for that. I swear by my Red Wings. I've had the same pair for four years, I just keep getting them resoled. There's this old cobbler downtown, one of the last guys who actually stitches the soles by hand instead of just gluing them. Gluing is so cheap, it peels right off the second you step in deep mud. We had a site last spring that was basically a mud pit. We actually had a mini-excavator sink right up to its tracks. Took two guys and a heavy-duty tow strap to yank it out. Those tow straps are incredible, though. They're made of this woven nylon that can hold, like, thirty thousand pounds without snapping. You have to be really careful, though, because if a strap that size snaps under tension, it acts like a giant whip. It can take a guy's head clean off. I saw a safety video about that once for a logging site. Logging is a crazy industry, man. Those guys are out in the middle of nowhere...\n\nBut, uh, what was I saying? Right, the list. So I'll have this list of follow-ups from the site walk, and I'll handle the first one or two things, and then I just get pulled into something else entirely. Like the stuck excavator, or whatever else is going on. And then days later I'll find out I never sent the email, or I completely forgot to call the subcontractor back, or I just never closed out the issue. And it's the exact same thing with chores at home. I'll start doing something and just... never finish it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder?\n\nPatient: No, no one's ever told me I had that. I mean, I never really went to the doctor much growing up anyway. My dad was one of those \"walk it off\" guys, you know? Unless a bone was sticking out, you were going to school. He worked at the auto plant for thirty-five years and I think he called in sick maybe twice. That plant closed down back in '08, which was a real shame because a lot of guys my dad's age just lost their pensions. They ended up turning the whole factory complex into these expensive loft apartments. I actually did some of the framing on that job. The original brickwork in those old factories is amazing, though. They used these solid clay bricks that you just can't find anymore. Nowadays everything is extruded and has holes in it to save weight and material. But those old solid bricks, man, they hold heat like you wouldn't believe. It makes the buildings really energy efficient in the winter, but in the summer, they turn into an absolute oven if you don't have good AC. We had to install these massive commercial HVAC units on the roof with a crane. Operating a crane that size is wild, the guy in the cab is basically using joysticks like a video game, but he's moving fifty tons of steel...\n\nBut, uh, no. To answer your question, I've never been diagnosed with anything like that. Never been treated for it, either. Just always been this way, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had any periods in your life where your symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity were not present, or were much less severe?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean, it's never really gone away, but it hasn't always been this bad. Like, it's been seriously disrupting my job for about two years and two months now. That's when the construction schedule changed and the hours just got completely chaotic. We started doing these split shifts to keep up with the supply chain delays. Supply chain stuff is a nightmare right now, by the way. You order a batch of electrical panels and they tell you it's a forty-week lead time. Forty weeks! How are you supposed to build a schedule around that? My buddy Mark, he's an electrician, he had to completely rewire this custom house because the homeowner decided last minute they wanted a smart home system. Those smart systems are crazy, you can control your thermostat from your phone while you're on vacation in Mexico. I went to Cabo once, back in my twenties. We rented dune buggies and drove them right on the beach. You have to lower the tire pressure so you don't get stuck in the soft sand. If you leave them fully inflated, they just dig a hole and you're buried to the axle in two seconds. It's basic physics, really, surface area and weight distribution...\n\nBut, yeah, anyway. They make you do all these tests, check your vision, your hearing, your blood pressure. Blood pressure is a big one, actually. A lot of guys in construction have terrible blood pressure because all we eat is fast food from the drive-thru or those roach coaches that pull up to the job sites. You know those food trucks? Some of them are actually pretty good now. There's this one guy, Hector, he makes these incredible al pastor tacos right on the spot. He's got the whole spit set up in the back of the truck with the pineapple on top. The acid in the pineapple actually tenderizes the pork as it cooks, it's brilliant. It's an old technique they brought over from Lebanese immigrants in Mexico, actually. They took the shawarma spit and adapted it for pork. Food history is fascinating when you really get into it. Like, did you know that tomatoes aren't originally from Italy? They're from the Americas. It's crazy to think about Italian food without tomatoes, but they didn't have them until the 1500s...\n\nBut, uh, anyway. No, I've never had a real, you know, comprehensive evaluation for this stuff. Just the basic physicals for work.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with any other mental health conditions, such as depression or anxiety?\n\nPatient: No, never anything like that. No depression, no anxiety, nothing they've ever put a name to, anyway. I mean, everybody gets stressed, right? Last week, we had this issue where the plumbers ran a three-inch PVC pipe right through a load-bearing joist. Just drilled a massive hole right in the middle of it. I almost lost my mind. I had to call the structural engineer out, and he was furious. Those engineers, man, they don't mess around. They calculate the sheer strength of the wood, the dead load, the live load.
